title: Super giant Cbus calls for SMSF restrictions
full_text:
Industry super fund giant Cbus is calling for restrictions on setting up self-managed super funds, including minimum balance requirements, to protect Australians from bad actors.
In an opinion piece published in The Australian, Cbus chief executive Kristian Fok warns people who leave APRA-regulated funds are leaving their safety net behind.
“Switch from a highly-regulated fund into an SMSF, and you carry all the risk. Losing your retirement savings is one of those risks, and there is no shortage of sharks, schemers and scammers out there willing to help you do just that,” Mr Fok writes.
The Shield and First Guardian fund failures, which led to more than 11,000 Australians losing a combined $1bn in superannuation, showed the impact of high-pressure sales tactics, he adds.
Most Shield and First Guardian investors were tipped into the two funds through platforms managed by super trustees such as Macquarie, Netwealth, Equity Trustees and Diversa. While exact SMSF figures have not been made public, an estimated $100m of the $500m First Guardian fund came from SMSFs.
To protect Australians from losing their nest egg and falling victim to unscrupulous actors, Cbus is calling for minimum balance requirements for SMSFs and maximum limits on advice fees that can be drawn from super accounts.
There are currently no such rules in place, though in the past, the securities regulator suggested $500,000 was the right amount to have in super before establishing an SMSF, in part due to the costs associated with self-managing super.
This recommendation was removed from ASIC’s guidance on SMSFs in 2023. The SMSF Association has suggested a balance above $200,000 is appropriate for anyone looking to manage their own retirement nest egg.
The call from the $92bn Cbus for restrictions on establishing SMSFs comes as more Australians are taking control of their super.
Self-managed funds had their highest growth rate in 12 years in 2025, bringing the total number of SMSF investors to 1.2 million.
But industry funds have recently warned of a spike in the number of Australians with small super balances moving away from APRA-regulated industry funds. Data released in February by industry super fund lobby, the Super Members Council, showed in the 2025 financial year, more than half of the Australians who left five of the major industry funds in favour of an SMSF had less than $100,000 in super.
The boost in SMSF numbers and shift away from industry funds comes after a torrid period for the for-profit funds.
The reputation-bruising scandals included excessive delays in paying out death benefits, and a cyber attack that targeted the major funds, including AustralianSuper. Consistently poor customer service from many of the major funds has also been blamed for the shift toward SMSFs and platforms used by financial advisers, such as HUB24 and Netwealth.
The ability of major funds to engage members on financial advice has been hampered by the delay in the rollout of the federal government’s financial advice reform package, Delivering Better Financial Outcomes.
The reforms, introduced in 2023, promised more affordable financial advice for Australians.
While the first tranche of the reforms were legislated in 2024, the trickier tranche-two changes that would allow lesser-qualified financial advisers to provide basic advice to super members has had minimal movement in the past year as the government focuses instead on consumer protections.
